canonicalExplanation.summary: React renders ordinary HTML, so all the accessibility rules still apply. Use **native elements** first: `<button>` for actions, `<a href>` for navigation, `<label>` for fields, `<dialog>` for modal dialogs. Native elements come with **roles, keyboard support and focus** built in. Give every control an **accessible name** (visible text, a label, or aria-label for icon buttons), and expose state with attributes such as `aria-expanded`, `aria-pressed` or `aria-invalid`. Test with a keyboard: Tab order, Enter/Space, Escape, and where focus goes when things open and close.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A "Report a problem" pop-up is built from divs: a div trigger with onClick, a div overlay, a close "×" span. Mouse users are fine; keyboard users can't open it, screen readers don't know it's a dialog, and Escape does nothing. A reusable dialog composes a real button trigger, labeled dialog region, focus management, and escape behavior. In this lesson you'll audit and repair component names, roles, states, focus order and keyboard behavior. ```predict {"question": "React handles clicks on any element. Is `
Report
` as good as a button?", "options": ["Yes, React makes it work", "No: it can't be focused with Tab, and Enter/Space and its role are missing"], "answer": 1, "why": "A native button gives focus, keyboard activation and the button role for free."} ```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Routing and application context** module, the **Remote data and asynchronous UI** module, your **Keyboard and accessibility-tree audit** skills, and **JSX expressions and attributes** (aria-* and htmlFor in JSX).

sections.heading: The model: native element, name, state, focus
Icon buttons

includes: Prefer native elements and give every control an accessible name and state.
Audit and repair keyboard behaviour and focus order, and test them.
excludes: Complex ARIA widgets like tree grids.

outcomes: Audit and repair component names, roles, states, focus order and keyboard behavior.

examples.title: A dialog everyone can use
examples.situation: A reusable dialog composes a real button trigger, labeled dialog region, focus management, and escape behavior.
walkthrough: **Real button trigger:** the div becomes `<button type="button">Report a problem</button>`, reachable by Tab.
**Labeled dialog region:** `<dialog aria-labelledby="report-title">` opened with showModal moves focus inside and closes on Escape.
**Test:** press Tab to the trigger, Enter to open, and a test will check the dialog is named "Report a problem"; Escape will close it and focus returns to the trigger.
examples.result: Keyboard and screen-reader users can open, use and close the dialog as easily as mouse users.

examples.title: The toggle that hid its state
examples.situation: A "Show answers" toggle changes colour when on, but screen-reader users can't tell whether answers are shown.
walkthrough: Colour was the only signal of state.
Change the text too: "Hide answers" when pressed.
examples.result: Everyone can tell whether answers are showing, by text and by announced state.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Because React handles events, div elements are preferable to native buttons.
misconceptions.correction: React only attaches handlers; it doesn't add focusability, keyboard activation or roles. Native buttons, links and form controls provide those automatically and should come first.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A dialog everyone can use", what couldn't keyboard users do with the div trigger?

analogy.example: Native elements are like **standard door handles**: everyone knows how to use them, including people who can't see them. A div with onClick is **a door you open by pressing a hidden panel**: it works if you already know where to press.
usefulFor: accessible name = the sign on the door
limitations: Doors don't announce themselves; buttons do, through their role and name.
A dialog is a room you enter and leave by the same door: focus in and back out.

steps.explanation: A real button trigger is reachable and activates with Enter.
The labeled dialog region receives focus management from showModal.
Escape behavior closes it and focus returns to the trigger.

trace.textAlternative: Walking the dialog with a keyboard. Step 1, Trigger: focus is button Report a problem; role is button. A real button trigger is reachable and activates with Enter. Step 2, Open: dialog name is Report a problem; focus is inside dialog. The labeled dialog region receives focus management from showModal. Step 3, Escape: dialog is closed; focus is trigger button. Escape behavior closes it and focus returns to the trigger.

faded.prompt: For "A dialog everyone can use", explain how a reusable dialog composes a real button trigger, labeled dialog region, focus management, and escape behavior.
expectedEvidence: Names the example "A dialog everyone can use": the trigger is a real button.
The labeled dialog region uses aria-labelledby.
Focus management and escape behavior come from showModal.
Keyboard and screen-reader users can open, use and close the dialog.

nearTransfer.prompt: Audit a card component where the whole card is a clickable div that navigates. Rewrite it with a real link covering the title, and keep any other buttons inside the card separate.
expectedEvidence: The link's name is the card title.

farTransfer.prompt: Audit three components in your app with a keyboard and a screen reader. Record name, role, state, keyboard and focus issues in a table, fix them, and add Testing Library tests using getByRole with names.
scaffold: Query by role and name in tests.

remediation.explanation: For every interactive element check five things: **name, role, state, keyboard, focus.** If you reached for a div, ask which native element already does the job.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The toggle that hid its state".

recap.summary: To audit and repair components, use native buttons, links, labels and dialog first, give every control an accessible name, expose state with aria attributes rather than colour, make everything work with Tab, Enter, Space and Escape, and manage focus into and back out of overlays, testing by role and name.
retrievalPrompts: Why is a native button better than a div with onClick?
How do you name an icon-only button?
Where should focus go when a dialog closes?
